title: KINCHO: Why Coils Last the Night—A Century of Materials | Brand Stories
description:
How does a handful of loose dried-flower powder become mosquito incense that can last the night? Follow more than a century of KINCHO's material choices: from postharvest drying, the trade-offs of chopping flowers and storing powder in an 1897 manual, to surviving wooden molds, hand-rolling equipment and factory processes, and finally to how you separate, place and light the coil. Materials and methods from different periods are explained through their respective sources. Historical scenes are original conceptual illustrations.

c05r001.text: You want a mosquito incense stick to last the night, but an early one burned out in about 40 minutes.

c05r002.text: In 1890, Eiichiro Ueyama launched stick-shaped mosquito incense, turning pyrethrum powder into thin sticks you could light.

c07o03.text: I thought the hard part was winding that circle. But the material faced a hurdle before it even became incense.

c07o04.text: What if days of rain follow the flower harvest? And once you light the incense, where does the ingredient escape?

c07o05.text: With this KINCHO coil, we'll follow more than a century of material choices, all the way to the end you light.

c07o06.text: How does a handful of loose dried-flower powder become a product that can see you through the night?

c07d01.text: First, you need usable powder. The company timeline says that in 1886, the seeds Eiichiro Ueyama received from America included pyrethrum.

c05r013.text: The timeline records the first harvest in 1887, along with experimental milling of pyrethrum powder.

c05le001.text: But think about it: from the same pyrethrum plant, why harvest and grind the flowers rather than all those leaves?

c05le002.text: The maker later explained that the active ingredients are mainly in the dried flowers, with almost none in the leaves and stems.

c07d02.text: When I read the Pyrethrum Cultivation Manual that Eiichiro Ueyama published later, I found another race against time after picking the flowers.

c07d03.text: The fifth edition describes thoroughly drying the fresh flowers, then making insect powder. But what if the weather won't cooperate?

c07d19.text: Its guide for sun-drying is four or five days of sunshine, with the flowers spread as thinly as possible. When are they ready to bring in?

c07d20.text: The book says to wait until the flower centers are dry before bringing them in. It warns that insufficient drying can cause discoloration after grinding.

c07d04.text: Imagine a small tray: there's room to spread the flowers out. But at peak harvest, how do you handle batch after batch?

c07d05.text: The book says some favor shade-drying, but the procedure can't keep up with large quantities of flowers, so sun-drying offers a more convenient option.

c07d07.text: If the rain keeps falling, the flowers are already in your hands. You can't just wait for clear skies. What backup does the manual offer?

c07d08.text: It describes making a wide bamboo screen and spreading the flowers on it, then supplying heat from below to dry them in a warm room.

c07d09.text: That gives the flowers somewhere to dry in wet weather. If you're in a hurry, they can also be chopped finely; the book says they then dry in about two or three hours.

c07d10.text: But faster drying comes at a cost. The publisher adds a note straight afterward: finely chopping the flowers somewhat weakens their potency.

c07d11.text: How are the dried flowers then processed into the insect powder sold in the book?

c07d12.text: When preparing it for sale, the book turns to pounding and sieving, making the dried flowers into fine powder.

c07d13.text: The sifted powder goes into bags or bottles. The flowers become goods you can hand to a buyer, rather than just a crop in the field.

c07d14.text: But what about powder you don't use up in a year? How does it wait until next time? Is leaving it lying around really enough?

c07d15.text: The manual's answer is to store it sealed in bottles or jars. Once it's powder, preservation takes over.

c07d16.text: The book also promotes its own fresh powder, complaining that some imports are two or three years old, or mixed with powdered stems and leaves.

c07d17.text: I see that as something sellers were competing over: what powder are you buying, and how has it been handled?

c07d18.text: A bag can contain the powder, but it can't arrange a whole night's burning for you. What shape would keep the material working?

c05r020.text: Those thin sticks from the opening borrowed the manufacturing method of incense used at Buddhist altars.

c05r021.text: But could those slender sticks reach you in one piece?

c05r023.text: One straight-stick product preserved by the maker is about 20 centimeters long. The record also says several were used at once.

c05r024.text: Lighting more sticks gives you more burning points, but does not lengthen the path along any one stick.

c05r025.text: Another problem came before delivery: the maker's factory account says thin, straight sticks broke easily in transit.

c05r026.text: To make a longer stick without needing a longer table, where could that thin strand go?

c07s02.text: In 1895, according to KINCHO's later account, Ueyama's wife proposed the spiral design.

c05r030.text: Imagine a cord: lay it straight, and the table must make room for its full length.

c05r031.text: Wind it inward, turn by turn: the path still follows the cord, but it takes up less flat space.

c05r032.text: I think this is an elegant turn. But does fitting a small table mean a factory can deliver it?

c07s03.text: The surviving wooden mold is registered as a prototype by the National Museum of Nature and Science. The idea was to fill its groove with material and push out a spiral.

c05r036.text: KINCHO's technical heritage page is explicit: the wooden mold was unsuitable for mass production and was never adopted.

c07s04.text: The company timeline records a patent application in 1900, then a market launch in 1902: seven years from idea to sale.

c05r049.text: I wanted to know how workers later turned those long strands into coils.

c05r050.text: The maker preserves an extruder used for hand-rolled coils, labeled as having entered use around 1910.

c07s05.text: A retrospective by a KINCHO author says the machine originally stood about two and a half meters tall. It's now preserved lying on its side.

c05le005.text: The National Museum of Nature and Science's record of this extruder says pyrethrum powder, powdered binder and other materials were first mixed with water into a clay-like mass.

c05r051.text: The machine squeezed the mass into long strands, which workers then cut to a set length. Where did they begin the first turn?

c05r052.text: Another product entry records workers bringing two strands together, then hand-winding them into a spiral around a small wooden core.

c05r054.text: Why did those two spirals have to stay together on their way to the shelf?

c05r055.text: KINCHO says the double-coil format reduces breakage in transit and transport costs.

c05r058.text: So what definite records of length and burn time remain for these later products?

c05r059.text: KINCHO's museum lists a coil from around 1919: about 58 centimeters long, burning for about 6 hours.

c05r061.text: The museum also lists a hand-rolled product from around 1922, burning about 12 hours. That is another product.

c05r067.text: If machines took over making the coils, did hand-rolling stop straight away?

c05r068.text: The company timeline records the completion of an automatic rotary die-cutting machine for spiral mosquito coils in 1940.

c05r071.text: I wondered whether the factory's raw materials were changing too, around this time.

c05r073.text: Materials changed too. KINCHO's factory account says pyrethrum cultivation shrank to increase food production.

c05r074.text: The same account says the synthetic ingredient allethrin was developed and put into use around 1955.

c05r076.text: In 1957, the company timeline records another completion: an improved, high-efficiency automatic die-cutting machine.

c05r069.text: The surviving hand-rolling equipment's catalogue entry says it remained in use until around 1957.

c07a01.text: You might wonder: how does extracting the active ingredients from flowers differ from grinding whole dried flowers into powder?

c07a02.text: A technical report from the National Museum of Nature and Science lists dried flowers as containing about 1 to 1.5 percent pyrethrins.

c07a03.text: The same passage says solvent extraction can yield a product containing about 20 percent. The material being handled is no longer simply dried flowers.

c07a04.text: To me, an easier mistake is to think of that active ingredient as a single substance that people had already fully identified.

c07a05.text: In a 2017 retrospective in Chemistry and Chemical Industry, a KINCHO author explained that natural pyrethrins are actually a mixture of six components.

c07a11.text: If you know which components are there, is their identity fully settled?

c07a06.text: Researchers knew the connections in the flat structure, but part of its three-dimensional arrangement was still unresolved. How could they pin that part down?

c07a07.text: In 1958, Yoshio Katsuda and colleagues transformed the material chemically to obtain a compound whose identity was known.

c07a08.text: The three-dimensional feature they were tracing survived the conversion. Following that link let them identify the original part's spatial arrangement.

c07a09.text: The article also reproduces a preserved lab notebook, captioned as having been used around that time. Behind the effect of that bowl of flowers was this kind of painstaking identification.

c07a10.text: These identity studies helped later development of synthetic ingredients move forward. But with a different active ingredient, could the plant powder be left out?

c05r091.text: The maker's current ingredient list still includes plant powders and wood flour.

c05rx005.text: The factory says those plant powders include the powder left after pyrethrum's active ingredients have been removed.

c05rx007.text: The maker also lists binding powders and starch.

c05r092.text: I didn't expect the maker's process guide to separate mixing from kneading: first, the powders spend about 30 minutes in a mixer.

c5r5a01.text: Green dye and water are added to that powder next. But the factory aims to use as little water as possible. How does it knead the mixture?

c5r5a02.text: Inside the kneading machine, a 400-kilogram drum crushes and kneads the material at the same time.

c5r5a03.text: According to this guide, kneading takes about 15 minutes. What condition must the mixture reach before it goes to the next machine?

c5r5a04.text: The maker gives a test you can feel: squeeze it in your hand, and it should retain finger marks. Only at that softness does it go to the extruder.

c5r5a05.text: Look at the outlet: a sheet emerges. The process page lists it as about 5 millimeters thick and 30 centimeters wide.

c05le010.text: In the maker's process, the sheet travels on a conveyor into the die-cutting machine, which works like a cookie cutter to cut out joined pairs of coils.

c5r5a06.text: But the shaped coils still contain close to 50 percent water at this point. The maker describes them as soft.

c5r5a07.text: Shipping has to wait. How much longer does this circle need to stay in the factory?

c5r5a08.text: The process page says the coils are placed on drying mesh, then naturally dried for two days in a drying room supplied with outdoor air.

c5r5a09.text: Then come quality checks for weight, burn time and active-ingredient content, followed by wrapping, inspection, boxing and shipping.

c07m03.text: How do you separate those two joined circles without damaging them before you even light them?

c05r080.text: Before use, the maker's current Q&A says to press gently at the center, then grip the thicker middle and ease the two coils apart vertically.

c05r081.text: What happens if you rush and grab the outer edge instead, pulling hard?

c05r082.text: Pulling hard from the outer edge can snap the incense coil.

c07u01.text: I'd also pay attention to the white mat in the holder supplied with the tin. What happens if you mistake it for packing material and pull it out?

c07u02.text: The maker's Q&A says it's a noncombustible fiberglass mat. The lit coil rests on it, so it stays in place during use.

c07u03.text: If the burning tip touches metal directly, the metal draws heat away and may extinguish it. Where the coil rests also affects how it burns.

c07u06.text: Turn the tin's lid over with the white mat facing up, so it can hold the lit coil. The maker also says to put the supplied cover in place.

c05r084.text: Once lit, why does the burning point move slowly along the incense?

c05r085.text: KINCHO's factory explains it through the cross-section: few gaps make it hard for oxygen to enter, so it burns slowly.

c05rx004.text: I'd like to ask: for the regular size you buy, what length and burn time does the maker list?

c05r088.text: For today's regular size, KINCHO lists one coil at about 75 centimeters, with a burn time of about 7 hours: a different generation of specifications.

c05r089.text: The maker also lists shorter- and longer-burning sizes, and burn times vary with the conditions of use.

c05rx009.text: As the burning point advances, how does the active ingredient leave the incense and enter the air?

c05rx010.text: The maker says the active ingredient continuously enters the air as extremely fine particles while the incense burns.

c05le012.text: The maker's explanation separates two locations. You can see the glowing tip, but must the active ingredient wait until it reaches that point to leave?

c07u04.text: The maker puts that glowing burning tip at about 700 to 800 degrees Celsius. The ingredient, though, volatilizes from the incense ahead of it.

c05le013.text: That location is about 6 to 8 millimeters from the tip, at about 250 degrees Celsius. It hasn't yet turned into the ash you can see.

c07u05.text: I'd leave the last stretch of the journey to the air. Once you light the coil, can you put it anywhere and expect the ingredient to reach every corner?

c07u07.text: The maker's Q&A uses the spread of smoke as a clue to the effective range. Placing the coil upwind helps the ingredient disperse with the airflow.

c07u08.text: For indoor use, the Q&A also explicitly calls for opening windows and maintaining ventilation. Once the coil reaches your room, the actual conditions still matter.

c05r101.text: Turning dried-flower powder into an overnight product means keeping material in place when it needs to stay, then letting it leave at a steady pace during use.

c05r102.text: If you've snapped a coil while separating a joined pair, tell me in the comments: did you grab the center or outer edge first?

c05r103.text: To explore the choices behind everyday objects that go beyond a single good idea, subscribe to this channel.
